items.question: Which TWO statements about how Claude Code permission rules are expressed are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Rules are matched against the model's stated intent for the step, so a rule can permit a class of goals rather than a class of concrete calls.
options.B: A rule may name a tool as a whole, or narrow it with a parenthesised specifier that constrains which uses of that tool it covers.
options.C: A rule set can only be defined once per machine, so per-repository permission differences must be handled by launching from different working directories.
options.D: Web fetching can be constrained by domain, so a rule can permit retrieval from named hosts while leaving others to be denied or prompted.
options.E: Adding an allow rule for a command removes any overlapping deny rule, since the two cannot coexist for the same command in one merged rule set.

items.question: A payments team maintains a service and a shared client library in two separate repositories checked out side by side. A migration requires changing both together, and engineers keep hitting a wall where the session can see the service but not the library. The team wants the pairing to work for everyone doing this migration, and wants file access to remain limited to those two trees.

options.A: Create a symbolic link from the service repository into the library checkout, so the library appears inside the working tree the session already has access to.
options.B: Run two sessions, one per repository, and have the engineer carry the relevant context between them by copying summaries across.
options.C: Switch the session to the permission mode that skips prompting, since the obstruction is a permission check and the engineer trusts both repositories.
options.D: Add the library checkout as an additional working directory, either per invocation from the command line or as a committed setting so the whole team gets it.

items.question: A team standardising on sandboxed command execution asks which developer platforms are covered natively. What is accurate?

options.A: Sandboxing is built on operating system primitives, so macOS and Linux are covered natively while a native Windows session needs a Linux subsystem, a dev container, or a virtual machine.
options.B: Sandboxing is implemented inside the CLI itself and behaves identically on macOS, Linux, and Windows, since the CLI inspects and rewrites each command before it is handed to the operating system.
options.C: Sandboxing is available only on Linux because it depends on a container runtime being installed, so macOS and Windows users must fall back on permission rules and manual review.
options.D: Sandboxing is a cloud-side feature applied to the model's proposed commands before they are returned to the client, so the local platform makes no difference to the guarantees.

items.question: A media conglomerate's platform group has built a Claude Code toolkit: four subagents, six slash commands, two skills, a formatting hook, and an MCP server pointing at the internal service catalogue. Twelve product teams across 60 repositories want it. Copying the files into each repository was tried for a month and produced eleven divergent copies. The group needs one version, updated centrally, adopted per repository rather than forced everywhere.

options.A: Publish the toolkit as a package and have each repository add a build step that copies the files into place at install time, so updates arrive whenever the dependency is bumped.
options.B: Push the whole toolkit through enterprise-managed policy settings so every machine in the company receives it automatically and no repository has to opt in.
options.C: Package the toolkit as a plugin published in a team marketplace, and have each adopting repository declare the marketplace and enable the plugin in its committed settings.
options.D: Move the toolkit into each engineer's personal configuration directory via a shared dotfiles repository, so it is available in every repository they open without per-repository work.

items.question: A defence contractor's security team proposes meeting an audit requirement — "the assistant must be prevented from reading files under the classified fixtures path in any repository" — by adding a blocking hook to the committed settings of all 30 repositories, with a CODEOWNERS rule protecting the file. An architect objects. What is the strongest basis for the objection?

options.A: Hooks add latency to every matching tool call, and across 30 repositories the cumulative slowdown will push engineers toward disabling them, so the control degrades over time.
options.B: The hook fires only after the read has completed, so the fixture's contents are already in the session before the hook can return a blocking decision.
options.C: Hooks committed to a repository cannot be written to reference an absolute path, so a single rule cannot cover a fixtures directory that sits outside each repository's tree.
options.D: The control lives in a file inside each engineer's working copy and takes effect only in a workspace the engineer has chosen to trust, so it can be edited or declined.

items.question: A clinical software team has a pre-execution hook that calls an internal policy service to decide whether a proposed command touches a validated system. A postmortem finds it stopped blocking anything for nine days: the policy service had moved endpoints, every call failed, and the hook script treated its own failure as a successful non-objection and returned a passing status. Nobody noticed because the outcome looked identical to a permitted command. The endpoint has now been corrected. What should the team do next?

options.A: Change the hook so that any internal error or unreachable dependency produces a blocking result rather than a passing one, and cache the policy locally so a transient outage does not halt all work.
options.B: Add structured logging and an alert that fires when the hook's error rate exceeds a threshold, so a recurrence is detected within minutes rather than after nine days.
options.C: Move the check from the pre-execution event to the post-execution event, where a failure to reach the policy service can be recorded against a command that has definitely run.
options.D: Pin the policy service endpoint in the hook's configuration and add a deployment check that fails the policy service's release if the endpoint changes.

items.question: An automotive supplier's repository has a well-maintained testing policy document under `docs/`, reviewed quarterly. When the team adopted Claude Code they summarised that policy into their root memory file. Six months later the two disagree in three places, and a code review used the memory file's stale version to justify a change. The team wants one source of truth without losing the guidance in the session.

options.A: Delete the testing section from the memory file and rely on the assistant reading the policy document when it needs it, since the document is discoverable in the repository.
options.B: Replace the summary in the memory file with a reference that imports the policy document, so the file the reviewers maintain is the file the session reads.
options.C: Keep both and add a quarterly checklist item to the policy review requiring the reviewer to update the memory file's summary in the same change.
options.D: Move the full policy text into the memory file and delete the document, so the guidance exists in exactly one place and is always in context.

items.question: A pharmaceutical group of 200 engineers must route all Claude Code traffic through its internal gateway, which applies prompt logging, data-loss inspection, and per-team budgets. Engineers work from home about half the week on split-tunnel VPN. Finance has also found several personal subscriptions being used for work. The group needs every session to go through the gateway and personal authentication to be unavailable, on and off the corporate network.

options.A: Add the gateway endpoint to the shell profile distributed by the configuration management agent, so the environment variable is set on every managed machine at login.
options.B: Block direct egress to the public endpoint at the corporate firewall and require engineers to connect to the full-tunnel VPN before starting any session.
options.C: Set the gateway endpoint and restrict the permitted login method through enterprise-managed policy settings, so both values are fixed at a layer engineers cannot edit.
options.D: Publish the gateway configuration in the onboarding guide and reconcile monthly by comparing gateway usage against the engineering headcount to find engineers who are bypassing it.

items.question: An MCP server is added at project scope. Where does the definition live, and who receives it?

options.A: In the user's home configuration, keyed by the project path, so it applies to that project on that machine only and is invisible to teammates.
options.B: In the running session's state only, so it is available until the session ends and must be re-added the next time the project is opened.
options.C: In the organisation's managed policy store, so it is distributed to everyone in the organisation whether or not they work on that project.
options.D: In a configuration file at the repository root, which is committed, so anyone who clones the repository receives the same server definition.

items.question: Which TWO statements about hooks are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A hook supplied by a repository runs on a teammate's machine only once that workspace has been trusted, so a fresh clone does not silently execute it.
options.B: Hooks run in a restricted execution context with no filesystem or network access beyond the tool call that triggered them.
options.C: Hooks execute as commands with the privileges of the user running the session, which makes an untrusted repository's hook configuration a supply-chain concern.
options.D: A hook defined in organisation-managed policy can be removed by an equivalent entry in a user-level settings file, since the more specific scope resolves last.
options.E: Hooks are limited to observing session activity and cannot influence whether an action proceeds.

items.question: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish skills, subagents, and slash commands in Claude Code? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A skill must enumerate every tool it needs, and a skill that omits a tool declaration is unable to make any tool call at all.
options.B: A skill's descriptive metadata is what is carried until it is used, with the body loaded only when the skill is actually invoked.
options.C: Where a project and a personal definition share a name, both are presented separately so the session can choose between them at call time.
options.D: Slash commands can only be defined in a user's personal configuration, so a repository cannot ship one to its contributors.
options.E: A subagent works in its own context window and returns a result to the calling session rather than sharing that session's conversation.

items.question: A robotics company is deploying a Claude Code job that reviews every pull request and posts comments. It runs on a shared runner with a token that can comment on and, technically, push to any repository in the organisation. Which TWO decisions correctly shape its permissions? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Enable prompt-skipping for the job, since a bot cannot answer a permission prompt and human reviewers will see anything wrong in the posted comments before it matters.
options.B: Grant the job the same permission set the engineers use, so its capabilities match what a human reviewer could do and behaviour is easy to reason about.
options.C: Allow only the reading and searching tools plus the specific command that posts a review, and grant nothing that writes to the working tree.
options.D: Grant broad allowances but cap the number of turns, so that anything harmful is bounded by how long the run is permitted to continue.
options.E: Add deny rules covering branch pushes and history rewriting, so that a later convenience allowance cannot quietly re-enable them.

items.question: A shipping software team is pruning a project memory file that has grown to 900 lines and is measurably crowding out working context. Which TWO items should stay? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A restatement of general engineering good practice — write tests, keep functions small, handle errors — so that the assistant works to a professional standard in this repository.
options.B: The exact invocation for the repository's non-standard test runner, which no amount of inspecting the tree reliably reveals.
options.C: A prohibition on reading the customer data fixtures, which the compliance team requires to hold even if an engineer edits this file.
options.D: A three-page summary of the system architecture, duplicating a design document that a separate group already maintains and reviews quarterly.
options.E: A list of the directories in this repository that hold generated artefacts and must never be hand-edited.

items.question: In a hook configured for a tool-related event, what does the matcher select?

options.A: Which tool calls the hook applies to, identified by tool name.
options.B: Which files on disk the hook is permitted to modify once it runs.
options.C: Which team members' sessions the hook applies to, so a hook can be scoped to a subset of the organisation.
options.D: Which model the hook applies to, so a policy can differ between capability tiers.

items.question: An external auditor will spend two weeks examining a rail operator's signalling codebase. They need to read widely, search, and run read-only analysis commands such as static analysis and dependency listing. They must not modify source, and the engagement letter states that modification must be structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. The operator wants the auditor productive on day one without a bespoke build of the tooling.

options.A: Give the auditor a checkout on a read-only filesystem mount, so that write attempts fail at the operating system level regardless of what the session tries to do.
options.B: Have the auditor work in the default permission mode and rely on the approval prompt for every write, since a prompt gives them an explicit chance to decline each modification.
options.C: Have the auditor work in the mode that automatically accepts edits, and take a git snapshot at the start so any modification can be reverted at the end of the engagement.
options.D: Provision the auditor's sessions in the exploratory permission mode, which permits reading and read-only commands, and add deny rules covering the file-writing tools.

items.question: A logistics company runs a nightly Claude Code job that can take 20 minutes. Twice it has hung and the orchestrator only discovered this at the job timeout, an hour later. The team wants their wrapper to surface progress while the run is in flight, detect a stall early, and still record a structured final result.

options.A: Keep plain text output and have the wrapper tail the stream, treating any two-minute gap in emitted characters as a stall signal.
options.B: Use the streaming structured output format, so the wrapper consumes events as they occur, times out on the absence of events, and reads the final result from the closing event.
options.C: Split the work into eight short invocations chained by the orchestrator, so progress is visible as each one completes and a stall is bounded by a single step's duration.
options.D: Keep the single structured result but have the job write heartbeat lines to a side file, which the orchestrator polls to distinguish a slow run from a stalled one.

items.question: Which TWO statements about how Claude Code memory files are scoped and composed are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Memory files located above the working directory in the directory tree are also considered for the session.
options.B: A memory file placed in a subdirectory replaces the repository root's memory file for any work done under that subdirectory.
options.C: Memory content is read once when the CLI is installed and cached until it is upgraded, so edits require a reinstall to take effect.
options.D: A memory file can pull in the contents of another file by reference, so shared guidance need not be duplicated.
options.E: A repository's memory file causes the engineer's personal memory file to be ignored for sessions opened in that repository.

items.question: A telco's on-call engineers use Claude Code in the platform repository during incidents. Two facts must accompany every request: the current incident identifier and whether a deploy freeze is active. Both come from an internal API and both can change during a single long session — a freeze can be declared mid-incident. Today engineers paste them manually and forget roughly a third of the time.

options.A: Record both facts in the repository memory file and update the file whenever the incident or the freeze status changes.
options.B: Add a slash command that fetches both values and states them, and ask engineers to run it whenever they believe the situation has changed.
options.C: Add a hook on the prompt-submission event that queries the internal API and attaches both current values as context to each request.
options.D: Add a hook on the session-start event that queries the API once and attaches both values, so every session begins with the correct state.

items.question: An insurer's platform team maintains a 60-line pre-execution hook that parses each proposed file operation and blocks anything under four infrastructure directories whose paths have not changed in three years. The hook has shipped two bugs — one let a write through for a week — it adds noticeable latency to every call, and its author left the company. A new engineer has been asked to make it more reliable.

options.A: Rewrite the hook in a compiled language and add a unit test suite covering the path-parsing logic, so both the latency and the correctness concerns are addressed.
options.B: Replace the hook with deny rules naming those four directories on the file tools, and keep hooks for checks that genuinely require running code.
options.C: Keep the hook but narrow its matcher to the file-editing tools and add a fast path that returns immediately when the target is outside the four directories.
options.D: Move the check to the post-execution event and have it revert any write that landed under one of the four directories, which removes the check from the latency-sensitive path.

items.question: A grocery retailer runs a single first-party monorepo with 80 engineers. Every MCP server defined in the repository's project configuration is added through a pull request reviewed by the platform group under a CODEOWNERS rule. Engineers hit an approval prompt whenever the platform group adds a server, several decline it by reflex, and then file tickets saying their tooling is broken. Engineers also clone third-party repositories for investigations.

options.A: Turn on automatic approval of repository-supplied servers in this monorepo's committed settings, so the platform group's reviewed additions arrive without a prompt while other repositories keep prompting.
options.B: Turn on automatic approval of repository-supplied servers in each engineer's personal settings, so the behaviour follows the engineer and does not have to be configured per repository.
options.C: Keep the prompt and add a step to the platform group's release notes announcing new servers, so engineers recognise the prompt when it appears and accept it.
options.D: Move the servers from the repository's project configuration to each engineer's personal configuration during onboarding, which removes the prompt because personal servers are not subject to it.

items.question: A memory file sits in a service subdirectory of a large repository. When does its guidance apply?

options.A: Only when the session is launched with that subdirectory as its working directory; opening the session at the repository root skips it entirely.
options.B: Always, on every session in the repository, exactly as if its contents had been appended to the root memory file.
options.C: Only after an engineer explicitly asks the session to load it, since files below the root are treated as optional reference material.
options.D: When the session works with files in that part of the tree, adding to the guidance already provided by memory files above it.

items.question: A gaming studio has a committed slash command that drafts release notes. It currently begins "Summarise the commits since the last release tag," and the results are inconsistent: sometimes the session inspects the right range, sometimes it guesses the tag, and occasionally it summarises the wrong fortnight. The team wants the command to always operate on the actual commit range.

options.A: Rewrite the instruction to spell out precisely how to find the last release tag and derive the range from it, so the session performs the same discovery steps on every run.
options.B: Have the command require the commit range as an argument, so the engineer looks up the two revisions and supplies them explicitly at invocation time.
options.C: Have the command execute the revision-listing command as part of its expansion, so the actual commit range is embedded in the prompt before the session sees it.
options.D: Add a hook that inspects each command before it runs and rewrites the session's history queries so they target the correct commit range.

items.question: Two engineers at a payments startup are working in the same repository on the same branch. One reports that her session runs the integration test command without asking; the other is prompted for approval every time and has started skipping the tests. Both are on current versions of the tooling. The team lead has been asked to sort it out before the sprint review.

options.A: Add the integration test command to the repository's committed allow rules immediately, since that is where the team wants the behaviour to be defined anyway.
options.B: Compare the effective configuration on both machines to identify which scope contributes the difference, then move the intended behaviour to the scope the whole team shares.
options.C: Have the engineer who is being prompted delete her local settings file, on the basis that a stale personal override is the most common cause of this divergence.
options.D: Raise it with the platform group as a candidate for organisational policy, so the command is permitted identically across every team in the company.

items.question: A chemicals manufacturer's engineering leadership wants to let 70 engineers run Claude Code with far fewer approval prompts, arguing that prompt fatigue is causing reflexive approvals. Which THREE must be in place before that change is made? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: An isolation boundary around sessions, so that actions taken without review cannot reach credentials, systems, or data outside the work at hand.
options.B: Deny rules covering credential paths and destructive operations, enforced at a scope individual engineers cannot lower.
options.C: A raised command timeout, so that autonomous runs are not interrupted partway through long operations and left in an inconsistent state.
options.D: A paragraph in each repository's memory file describing the boundaries the assistant is expected to respect while operating with reduced prompting.
options.E: Retained records of what each session did, held where the team can reconstruct a run after the fact.

items.question: A public broadcaster rolled out sandboxed command execution with a default-deny outbound network policy. Within two days, dependency installation was failing for every engineer because the package registry was unreachable from inside the sandbox. The platform lead is under pressure to disable sandboxing before the end of the week.

options.A: Disable the sandbox for the commands that install dependencies, keeping it in force for every other command the session runs during the build.
options.B: Vendor all dependencies into the repositories so installation never needs network access, which removes the conflict permanently for every team.
options.C: Have engineers run dependency installation manually in an unsandboxed terminal before each session starts, leaving the session itself fully sandboxed for the task.
options.D: Keep default-deny and add explicit network allowances for the package registry and the internal proxy, so the traffic the build needs is permitted.

items.question: A health insurer added a hook that runs the repository's type checker to catch broken edits early. It was configured without a matcher, so it fires on every tool call — including reads and searches — and the type checker takes four seconds on this codebase. Engineers have started removing the hook from their local configuration, and the tech lead has evidence that broken edits are reaching review again.

options.A: Match the hook to the file-editing tools and have it exit immediately when the edited file is outside the type checker's scope, so the cost falls only on real edits.
options.B: Keep the hook unmatched but cache the type checker's results, so repeated calls within a session return quickly after the first invocation pays the full cost.
options.C: Move the check to the end of the turn so it runs once per response rather than once per tool call, accepting a coarser signal in exchange for far less per-call overhead.
options.D: Deploy the hook through organisational policy so engineers cannot remove it from their own configuration, which restores the guarantee the tech lead has lost.

items.question: A wrapper script must reliably detect that a non-interactive Claude Code run failed. What should it check?

options.A: Whether the output contains words such as error or failed, since a failing run explains the problem in its response text.
options.B: The process exit status, using the structured output for detail about what went wrong.
options.C: Whether the output is empty, since a successful run always produces text and a failed one produces nothing.
options.D: The elapsed wall-clock time against an expected duration, since failures terminate faster than successful runs.

items.question: Which TWO statements about how a non-interactive Claude Code run is configured are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A non-interactive run ignores deny rules, because deny is enforced by declining a prompt and no prompt can be shown.
options.B: The set of tools available can be constrained for a single run from the command line, independently of what the settings files on the machine contain.
options.C: A non-interactive run is limited to the directory it was launched from and cannot be given additional working directories.
options.D: Configuration resolves through the same precedence chain as an interactive session, so organisational policy still applies.
options.E: Non-interactive mode automatically switches to the prompt-skipping permission mode when no terminal is attached, so that runs never block.

items.question: A civil engineering software team has a bespoke test harness invoked through a wrapper script rather than the language's usual runner. Claude Code sessions across the team keep reaching for the conventional runner, which fails confusingly. There is no security concern; the team simply wants everyone's sessions to use the right command.

options.A: Add a deny rule for the conventional runner, so the wrong command fails immediately and the session is forced to look for an alternative.
options.B: Add a pre-execution hook that detects the conventional runner and rewrites the call to invoke the wrapper script instead.
options.C: State the correct invocation in the repository's committed memory file, so every session in the repository has the convention in context.
options.D: Ask engineers to mention the wrapper script in their first message whenever they expect the session to run tests.

items.question: A staffing platform's team merged a change adding a formatting hook to the repository's committed settings. Since the merge, every teammate's session reports a hook failure on each edit, because the hook invokes a binary at a path that exists only on the author's machine. The author is on leave. Work is continuing but the failures are noisy and two engineers have started ignoring all hook output. What should the team do next?

options.A: Change the hook to invoke the formatter through the repository's own tooling, and add a CI check that exercises the committed configuration in a fresh checkout.
options.B: Revert the merge to restore the previous configuration, and reopen the change when the author returns from leave and can test it on a colleague's machine.
options.C: Document the required binary in the repository's setup instructions and ask each engineer to install it, since the hook is correct and the environments are incomplete.
options.D: Move the hook from the committed settings into the author's personal configuration, so it stops affecting teammates while remaining available to whoever wants it.

items.question: How does the permission mode that automatically accepts file edits differ from the mode that skips permission prompting altogether?

options.A: They are equivalent in effect; one is simply an older name for the other, retained so that existing configuration continues to work.
options.B: The edit-accepting mode still confirms file modifications but stops confirming shell commands, on the basis that commands are the reversible operation of the two.
options.C: The edit-accepting mode auto-approves file modifications while other tool calls remain subject to the permission layer; the prompt-skipping mode removes the confirmation step across the board.
options.D: The edit-accepting mode applies only to files the session itself created during that session, so modifications to pre-existing files continue to be confirmed individually.

items.question: An engineer at a mapping company has an allow rule covering the repository's build script. She is puzzled that a proposed command chaining the build script with a cleanup step that deletes a directory tree is not permitted outright, since the chain begins with something she explicitly allowed. What is the correct explanation?

options.A: The parts of a chained command are evaluated separately, so an allowance covering one part does not authorise the others in the chain.
options.B: Chained commands are never matched by allow rules at all, so any command containing a chaining operator always requires confirmation regardless of its contents.
options.C: The allowance did not apply because the rule matched only when the build script is the entire command, and any additional argument or text after it breaks the match.
options.D: Chained commands are matched against the last element of the chain, since that is the operation whose effect persists after the command completes.

items.question: A deny rule names a tool without any parenthesised specifier. What is the effect?

options.A: Only invocations of that tool which themselves carry no arguments are refused; calls with arguments fall through to the remaining rules.
options.B: The tool is downgraded to always prompting, so the engineer decides case by case rather than the call being refused outright.
options.C: The denial applies only within the configuration scope where the rule was written, so an allow rule in a different scope reinstates the tool there.
options.D: All uses of that tool are refused, regardless of arguments, and no allow rule elsewhere reinstates it.

items.question: A utility company's incident triage job uses Claude Code non-interactively against an MCP server for its ticketing system. The server exposes tools that read tickets and search history, and also tools that transition a ticket's state and post to customer-visible fields. The triage job must read and summarise only; a customer-visible post from an automated job would be a regulatory notification issue. The ticketing team is not willing to run a second server instance.

options.A: Allow the server as a whole and add an instruction to the job's prompt stating that it must only read and must never transition or post to a ticket.
options.B: Allow the specific read and search tools by name and deny the state-transition and customer-visible tools, so the mutating operations are unreachable from this job.
options.C: Allow the server as a whole and rely on the ticketing system's own permissions by giving the job's service account read-only rights in that system.
options.D: Configure the server at a scope the job does not read, so the triage job simply has no connection to the ticketing system and works from an exported snapshot instead.

items.question: An engineer at an airline is mid-way through a delicate refactor, with a lot of accumulated reasoning in the session about which call sites have been converted. She now needs to know every place a deprecated currency formatter is referenced across a 400,000-line codebase — an exhaustive search that will read dozens of files and produce far more intermediate output than the answer requires. She does not want to lose the refactor's state.

options.A: Delegate the search to a subagent, which does the work in its own context and returns the list of call sites to the current session.
options.B: Package the search procedure as a skill and invoke it, so the search steps load on demand rather than being described inline.
options.C: Compact the current session first to free room, then run the search in the same session with the refactor state summarised.
options.D: Open a second session in a separate terminal to run the search, then paste the resulting list back into the refactor session.

items.question: Which TWO statements about Claude Code plugins are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A plugin must be installed by each engineer individually; a repository has no way to declare which plugins it expects contributors to have.
options.B: A plugin can bundle subagents, slash commands, skills, hooks, and MCP server definitions together under a single version.
options.C: Plugins are limited to slash commands, so agents, skills, and hooks must be distributed through some other channel.
options.D: A repository can declare in its committed settings both the marketplace it draws plugins from and which plugins should be enabled.
options.E: Enabling a plugin in a repository allows it to override organisational policy for any settings key the plugin defines.

items.question: A retail bank's regulator asks a question about a change merged eight months ago: what controls were in force on the assistant that helped produce it, and could it have read the customer data fixtures at that time? The team can produce the pull request and the reviewers, but their answer about configuration is that they believe the rules were the same as today. The head of engineering wants to be able to answer this precisely for future enquiries.

options.A: Begin retaining full session transcripts for seven years in the compliance archive, so a future enquiry can be answered by reading what the assistant actually did during the work.
options.B: Have each engineer record, in the pull request description, which permission rules and hooks were active on their machine when they made the change.
options.C: Turn on verbose diagnostic output across the fleet and ship it to the central log platform, so configuration details appear in the logs from now on.
options.D: Keep the governing configuration in version control alongside the code — settings, hook scripts, agent and skill definitions, and pinned versions of shared tooling.

items.question: An engineer at a hotel booking company built a subagent in her personal configuration that plans database migrations against their unusual schema conventions. It works well, three teammates asked for it, and she sent them the file. Two of them have since edited their copies, and a fourth engineer is now getting different advice from what everyone assumed was the same agent. The team wants one version that everyone gets, including new joiners.

options.A: Publish the definition on the team wiki as the canonical version and ask the two engineers who edited their copies to reconcile their changes against it.
options.B: Distribute the definition through organisational policy so every engineer receives an identical copy that cannot be altered locally.
options.C: Commit the definition to the repository's agents directory, where it is reviewed like code and takes precedence over the personal copies teammates still have.
options.D: Have the author keep ownership of the definition and send an updated file to the team whenever she improves it, with a version number in the filename.

items.question: A team's MCP server definition is committed at project scope and the server requires a per-developer token. How should the token be handled?

options.A: Reference an environment variable in the committed configuration, so each machine supplies its own value at run time.
options.B: Commit the token encrypted and have a start-up step decrypt it, so the committed file never contains a readable secret.
options.C: Commit a shared team token and restrict access to the repository, so the credential is protected by the repository's own permissions.
options.D: Have each developer copy the committed definition into their personal configuration and add their token to their private copy.

items.question: A fintech's monorepo contains both a marketing site and the card-authorisation service, which is in PCI scope and subject to much stricter handling rules. Splitting the repository has been rejected on delivery grounds. Which TWO decisions correctly shape the Claude Code configuration? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Split the monorepo after all, since a single configuration cannot express different rules for different parts of one tree.
options.B: Keep repository-wide conventions in the root memory file and put the card-authorisation handling rules in a memory file inside that service's directory.
options.C: Rely on memory scope to limit access, since a session working in the marketing subtree will not reach the card-authorisation subtree.
options.D: Give each team a personal settings file encoding its own restrictions, so the rules follow the engineer rather than the part of the tree being worked on.
options.E: Express the card-authorisation restrictions as path-scoped deny rules, which apply wherever in the tree the session happens to be working.

items.question: An analytics team wired a non-interactive Claude Code call into their local pre-push hook to summarise the outgoing diff for the pull request description. It usually takes 15 seconds. Twice it has run for several minutes and blocked the push entirely, once when the engineer was offline. The team values the local convenience and their CI already runs the same summary as an authoritative step.

options.A: Remove the local call, since CI already produces the summary and duplicating it locally adds a failure mode without adding value.
options.B: Keep it unbounded but run it in the background and attach the summary to the pull request when it eventually finishes, so the push is never delayed.
options.C: Make the push depend on the summary succeeding, so an engineer cannot push work whose description was not generated, and raise the timeout to accommodate slow runs.
options.D: Bound the call with a short timeout and a turn limit, and have the hook allow the push to proceed when the call does not complete or cannot reach the network.

items.question: How do permission rules and operating-system sandboxing divide responsibility in Claude Code?

options.A: Sandboxing supersedes permission rules where both are configured, since operating-system enforcement is stronger and the two would otherwise conflict on every call.
options.B: Permission rules are advisory guidance to the model about which tools to prefer, while sandboxing is the only mechanism that actually refuses anything.
options.C: Permission rules decide which tool calls may be made at all, while sandboxing constrains what a command that was permitted can reach on the filesystem and the network.
options.D: Permission rules govern local tools and sandboxing governs MCP servers, so the two apply to disjoint categories and never interact.

items.question: A 15-person team at a scooter-hire company reports approving roughly 40 prompts a day each, almost all for the same handful of build, test, lint, and package-manager commands. Approval has become reflexive, and last week someone approved a command that removed an untracked configuration directory. The lead has a week to change this and is not willing to reduce the team's real protection.

options.A: Allow the shell tool as a whole for this repository and rely on the deny rules already covering the most destructive commands to catch anything dangerous.
options.B: Enumerate the repository's build, test, lint, and package-manager commands as allow rules in the committed settings, keep destructive commands denied, and leave the rest prompting.
options.C: Switch the team's default to the mode that automatically accepts file edits, which removes the largest single source of interruption in the day without touching command execution at all.
options.D: Run a one-week trial with prompting disabled, measure whether anything harmful occurs, and then decide how much protection the team genuinely needs.

items.question: A logistics group has acquired a smaller company and inherited a 12-year-old codebase with two remaining maintainers and almost no documentation. Six engineers are being onboarded onto it next month and will use Claude Code from day one. The group wants useful repository guidance in place before they arrive, without waiting for anyone to spend a month reading the code.

options.A: Use the initialisation command to generate a first-draft memory file from the codebase, then have the two maintainers prune and correct it before it is committed.
options.B: Wait until the six engineers have worked in the codebase for a month, then have them write the memory file from what they learned, so it reflects real difficulties rather than a machine's summary.
options.C: Copy the memory file from the group's most architecturally similar codebase and adjust the obviously wrong parts, so the six engineers start with familiar conventions.
options.D: Skip repository guidance for now, since an inaccurate memory file is worse than none and the codebase is not yet understood well enough to describe.

items.question: Before working in an unfamiliar repository, an engineer wants to know what hooks will run in the session. What does the hooks view give them?

options.A: It executes each configured hook once against a sample event so the engineer can observe what each one actually does before starting work.
options.B: It lists only the hooks defined by this repository, since hooks from personal and organisational configuration are managed separately and shown elsewhere.
options.C: It shows which hooks are configured for each event and which configuration source supplied each one.
options.D: It is the only place hooks can be defined, so what it shows is by definition everything that will run in the session.

items.question: A conglomerate's platform group publishes a shared Claude Code toolkit that twelve product teams have adopted. On Tuesday they published an update that changed a hook's behaviour, and by mid-morning all twelve teams were blocked on the same failure. The immediate cause is understood and a corrected version is ready. The head of platform engineering wants to know what changes so this cannot recur at this scale.

options.A: Add an automated test suite to the toolkit that exercises every hook, agent, and command against a fresh checkout before publication, so a defect of this kind is caught upstream.
options.B: Have each adopting team disable the toolkit's hooks locally when a problem occurs, and publish a documented procedure so they can do it within minutes.
options.C: Withdraw the shared toolkit and let each product team own its own copy of the artefacts, so a single publication can never affect twelve teams simultaneously.
options.D: Restore the previous version for the affected teams, then change adoption so repositories move to a new version deliberately, with one team taking each release first.

items.question: During a review at a healthcare analytics company, an engineer notices that the repository's committed settings contain an allow rule granting the shell tool with no restriction. Version history shows it was added 14 months ago by someone who has left, with the commit message "stop the constant prompting". The team of 20 has been working under it since, with no known incident.

options.A: Remove the rule immediately, since it is plainly over-broad, and let the team re-add specific allowances as they encounter prompts over the following days.
options.B: Determine which commands the team actually runs, replace the blanket rule with allowances covering those, and land the narrowing as one reviewed change.
options.C: Leave the rule in place and add deny rules for the destructive commands the team can think of, which addresses the real risk without disrupting anyone's workflow.
options.D: Escalate to the security group to have shell execution restricted through organisational policy, since the repository clearly cannot be trusted to manage its own permissions.

items.question: An internal audit function is reviewing how a 200-engineer organisation governs Claude Code. Which THREE properties should the setup have to withstand that review? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Controls that must not be declined are expressed in organisation-managed policy rather than in files inside the repositories they govern.
options.B: Every engineer signs an annual attestation confirming they have not weakened their local configuration.
options.C: Repository configuration is committed, so the rules in force at any past commit can be reconstructed from version history.
options.D: Approval prompting is enabled for every tool everywhere, since a human confirming each action is the strongest evidence of control that can be produced.
options.E: Activity from automated runs is retained where a reviewer can reconstruct what a given run did.

items.question: A freight forwarder classifies customs declarations with a five-step chain: OCR extraction, a Haiku normalisation call, a tariff-rule retrieval, a Sonnet classification call, and a deterministic validator. Each of the five services emits structured logs with its own internally generated request id, retained 90 days. A customer disputes a single HS code assigned three weeks ago; an engineer spent two days grepping logs to reconstruct which retrieved rule the model saw. What change most directly prevents the next two-day reconstruction?

options.A: Increase log retention from 90 days to seven years so that a late-arriving dispute always has a complete body of evidence available to search through.
options.B: Have every service log the full prompt and response payload it sent to Claude, so that any single log line can be interpreted without reference to the others.
options.C: Mint one trace id at the edge, propagate it through all five steps, and persist it on the customer-visible classification record so a case number resolves straight to its spans.
options.D: Collapse the five steps into a single Sonnet call with extended thinking, so each classification produces one log record instead of five that have to be stitched together.

items.question: A Claude call in production produced a bad output that the team cannot reproduce from the user's original input. Which captured set is the minimum needed to attempt a faithful replay?

options.A: The user's original input text, the name of the prompt template that was in use at the time, and the wall-clock timestamp recorded for the request.
options.B: The model's response text, its stop reason, and the input and output token counts recorded for the request.
options.C: The deployed application version, the customer account identifier, and the distributed trace id attached to the request.
options.D: The fully rendered prompt exactly as sent, the resolved model identifier, the sampling parameters, and every tool result injected mid-turn.

items.question: A media group routes all Claude traffic through one shared internal gateway on a single provider account. Finance receives a single monthly invoice, and each of eight product teams insists its share is small. The gateway already authenticates callers with per-service API keys and logs status code and latency for every request. No product team has capacity to change its call sites this quarter. Which TWO changes give finance defensible per-team attribution? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Have finance divide the monthly invoice equally across the eight teams and true it up each quarter using a sampled traffic study.
options.B: Record input, output and cache-read token counts per request at the gateway, keyed to the calling service key, and price them against the same rate table finance uses to reconcile the invoice.
options.C: Require every team to add a `team` field to the request body so the gateway can group spend by owner without maintaining any extra state.
options.D: Maintain a registry mapping each service key to an owning team and cost centre, and stamp that owner onto every request the gateway logs.
options.E: Alert when the gateway's aggregate monthly spend crosses a threshold so that overruns surface before the invoice arrives rather than after.

items.question: A 140-engineer platform organisation rolled out AI coding assistance and now reports "AI-assisted lines accepted per engineer per week" to its VP as the headline adoption KPI. The figure has tripled in a quarter and is being used to justify the next year's licence spend. A staff engineer objects to the metric. Which objection is the strongest case for replacing it?

options.A: Line counts are not normalised across languages, so a team migrating from Java to Python would show a decline that has nothing to do with how much assistance it received.
options.B: Accepted lines measure production volume, not delivered value; the figure rises when engineers accept verbose or duplicated code, and nothing in it separates that from real throughput.
options.C: Acceptance events are recorded client-side and are lost when an editor session crashes, so the reported figure systematically understates the assistance engineers actually took.
options.D: The metric covers only assistant users and omits engineers who call the API from their own scripts, so cross-team comparisons draw on an incomplete population.

items.question: Which property most distinguishes a prompt library kept as versioned code in the application repository from one kept in a runtime configuration store?

options.A: The template and the code that consumes it move together through review, CI evals and rollback, so a deployed build cannot pair new code with a stale prompt.
options.B: Prompt changes take effect without a redeploy, shortening the loop between spotting a bad output in production and shipping a corrected instruction.
options.C: Prompt text is encrypted at rest and access-controlled, so only reviewers holding repository permissions can read the instructions running in production.
options.D: Per-prompt token cost is computed automatically at commit time, giving the team a spend forecast before a change is allowed to reach production.

items.question: A health insurer rolls out a Claude-drafted claim-denial explanation behind a percentage flag. The automation promotes 5% to 25% to 100% if, for 60 minutes at each stage, HTTP error rate stays under 0.5%, p95 latency stays under 3 seconds, and no pod restarts occur. In a staging rehearsal the feature was promoted all the way to 100% while producing fluent explanations that cited the wrong policy clause in roughly one denial in six. What is the fundamental defect in the gate?

options.A: Sixty minutes at 5% of traffic does not accumulate enough requests for the error-rate threshold to be statistically meaningful, so the first promotion is effectively unguarded.
options.B: Percentage flags assign users at random, so the 5% cohort is unlikely to contain the unusual claim types on which the model's clause selection actually fails.
options.C: A 3-second p95 threshold conceals the tail; some members wait long enough on p99 to abandon the flow before an explanation ever renders.
options.D: Every signal in the gate measures whether the service responded. A wrong explanation is a successful response, so no promotion criterion can observe correctness at all.

items.question: At 02:10 a telco's Claude-powered outage-notification summariser begins producing summaries that omit the affected region, which downstream systems use for routing. Error rate, latency and token usage are all normal. No deploy has shipped in 36 hours and the prompt template is pinned in the release artefact. The on-call engineer has the full trace of one bad request open. What is the most useful next step?

options.A: Roll back the most recent application deploy to restore known-good behaviour, then investigate the cause once summaries are correct again.
options.B: Raise the summariser from Haiku to Sonnet and observe whether the region reappears, since the omission looks like a capability limit under load.
options.C: Diff the rendered prompt in the bad trace against the rendered prompt from a known-good trace earlier the same day, field by field.
options.D: Open a provider support ticket reporting a suspected model regression and hold all changes until the provider confirms or denies it.

items.question: Within an AI feature's request path, which practice most directly prevents a live credential that appears at runtime from being persisted somewhere it can be read later?

options.A: Redact secret-shaped values from prompts, tool results and trace payloads before those payloads are written to the logging, tracing and eval stores.
options.B: Rotate every service credential on a 30-day schedule so that any value which does leak has a strictly bounded window of usefulness to an attacker.
options.C: Hold all credentials in a managed secrets manager and inject them into the container as environment variables at process start rather than committing them.
options.D: Require a second reviewer on any commit touching a path on the repository's secrets-adjacent file list, so no credential change merges unnoticed.

items.question: A public-sector agency's grants-triage service has grown to 31 prompt templates, 9 tools and an evaluator step. New engineers take six to eight weeks before they can change a prompt without supervision. The recurring failure is identical: someone edits a template, unit tests pass, and an eval nobody knew existed regresses, discovered days later in the weekly report. The tech lead has one sprint of capacity. Which action produces the largest reduction in time-to-safe-change?

options.A: Write an architecture document covering all 31 templates, the 9 tools and how the evaluator scores each output, and require new joiners to read it in week one.
options.B: Pair every new engineer with a senior for their first four weeks of prompt work so that risky edits are caught before they are proposed.
options.C: Consolidate the 31 templates into roughly 8 by parameterising near-duplicates, so a newcomer has substantially less surface area to understand.
options.D: Wire the eval suite into the pull-request check so that any template edit reports its own before-and-after scores directly on the diff.

items.question: An energy retailer's tariff-comparison assistant is a Sonnet agent with four tools over a live tariff database. Across two weeks, about 3% of sessions end with the assistant confidently quoting a tariff withdrawn last year. No errors are logged, the final answers are well formed, and the team has complete traces including every tool call and every tool result. Where should the investigation start, and on what reasoning?

options.A: At the model's final synthesis turn, because a confident wrong answer produced from correct inputs is by definition an instruction-adherence problem in the closing step.
options.B: At the tool results inside the failing trajectories, because a withdrawn tariff reaching the answer most often means it was retrieved and handed to the model as current context.
options.C: At the sampling parameters, because non-zero temperature is the mechanism by which two otherwise identical sessions can settle on different tariffs.
options.D: At the deployed system prompt, comparing it against the version in the repository, because drift between the two explains behaviour changes with no accompanying code change.

items.question: A team is instrumenting each Claude call in its chain as a span in an existing distributed tracing system. Beyond the standard timing and status fields the tracer already records, which TWO span attributes most improve the team's ability to explain a specific bad output months after it happened? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A stable identifier for the prompt template together with its version, so the exact instruction text can be recovered from the repository at any later date.
options.B: The endpoint's p95 latency over the preceding five minutes, sampled at the moment the call was issued, to give each span its own local baseline.
options.C: The wall-clock duration of the call, broken out into time-to-first-token and total elapsed time so streaming behaviour can be analysed.
options.D: The resolved model identifier actually served for the call, rather than the alias the client requested at call time.
options.E: The full raw response body, stored inline as a span attribute so an investigator never has to follow a reference to a second store.

items.question: A logistics scale-up is building a replay harness so any production Claude request from the last 30 days can be re-run against a candidate prompt change before it ships. Which THREE properties must the harness have for its verdicts to be trustworthy? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: It replays the tool results captured at the original request time rather than re-invoking the live tools during the replay.
options.B: It forces temperature to zero on every replay so the harness is deterministic and any two runs are exactly comparable.
options.C: It pins the model identifier recorded on the original request, and reports explicitly when that version is no longer available to serve.
options.D: It replays only requests that produced an error or a low user-feedback score, since successful requests carry no diagnostic value for a prompt change.
options.E: It runs each case more than once and reports the spread, because one sample cannot distinguish a real regression from ordinary sampling variation.
